title: Katamari Damacy: a school prototype that turned scale into the whole game
summary: Keita Takahashi's team built simple dual-stick control and a strict object hierarchy into a rolling system whose mechanical escalation became comedy and spectacle.

sourceLabels.katamari-gdc: Katamari Damacy: rolling from prototype to product

blocks.text: The idea survived by being playable

Katamari Damacy grew from a prototype developed with Namco's digital-art school context, where Keita Takahashi's unusual rolling concept could be tested before it resembled a conventional product. The prototype established the important fact early: pushing a ball through a cluttered world and hearing objects attach was satisfying without a large story or complex combat system.

Both analog sticks moved in parallel to roll forward or backward; opposing them turned the katamari, and quick gestures triggered dashes or pivots. The mapping made the controller resemble two hands pushing a sphere. It was initially unfamiliar but internally consistent, allowing the game to avoid a camera-and-character scheme that would separate the player from the rolling object.
Every object needed a place in the hierarchy

The katamari could collect only objects below an allowed size, so thousands of props needed dimensions, collision, attachment points and categories. A pencil, cat, person and building were not merely decorations; each occupied a rung in progression. Bad scale data could block movement or make a joke arrive too early, turning asset management into game balance.

Collected objects protruded from the ball and changed how it rolled until they were buried by later layers. The system had to add collision and visual complexity without becoming unstable as the count grew. Simplified shapes, object limits and selective simulation preserved the comic irregularity while keeping the PS2 able to draw the expanding mass.

A room that began as a maze around table legs later became a small patch beneath the katamari. Levels guided players across thresholds into new zones, using familiar objects as rulers for progress. The sensation of growth came less from a number in the interface than from relationships reversing around the player.

Objects announced themselves through pops, voices and musical layers, turning constant acquisition into rhythmic feedback. The eclectic soundtrack matched the game's refusal of realism and gave repeated rolling a changing emotional pace. Audio also confirmed a pickup even when the object vanished into a visually chaotic ball.
A small production with a huge cultural silhouette

Katamari's commercial scale was modest, but its visual language was instantly recognizable and translated naturally into fan art and costume. The game demonstrates how a focused prototype can organize controls, assets, technology and humour around one verb. Its escalation feels extravagant because the underlying rule remains simple enough to understand at every size.
